source.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
source.authors: Alexandru Damian; Eshaan Nichani; J. Lee

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is supplied.
record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes and empirically tracks full-batch gradient descent at the edge of stability, reporting loss and sharpness behavior relevant to V5. Its predicted-dynamics analysis is a different method from the original observations.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports training accuracy in Figure 6, but the supplied text does not describe its values; the figure-only plot does not establish the zero-training-error behavior in V1. References to other studies' results are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study explicitly replicates Cohen et al.'s full-batch gradient-descent experiments, measuring training loss and Hessian sharpness at the edge of stability. Its additional theoretical analysis does not make these empirical replications a different-method test. It is not an original source for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct: self-stabilization explains bounded edge-of-stability dynamics through curvature reduction, and experiments support tracking a sharpness-constrained trajectory while loss decreases over longer times. Larger learning rates accelerate convergence in the reported ResNet18 experiment. Qualify the conclusion: the theorem establishes local coupling under assumptions, not global convergence; generalized dynamics accommodate sharpness offsets from 2/η.
record.recipe_differences: Full-batch gradient descent and edge-of-stability measurements are close to the cited Cohen et al. setup, while this paper focuses on predicted dynamics and constrained-trajectory comparisons. The ResNet18 learning-rate sweep is an additional experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Learning rate varies across experiments. The paper also reports that the standard cubic predictions can fail when assumptions are violated, including for ResNet18 and logistic-loss settings; generalized predictions track the tested settings more broadly.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger learning rates improve ResNet18 test accuracy in Figure 6.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger learning rates during full-batch training can improve generalization on CIFAR-10.

record.problems: Experiments are on selected models and datasets, with training stopped when the second Hessian eigenvalue reaches 1.9/η to maintain the single-unstable-eigenvalue setting. Numerical values for the plotted results are not stated in the text, and uncertainty estimates are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results with stated numeric values were omitted. Figure 6 accuracy is retained as a row, but it does not measure training classification error.

untested.parts: Zero or near-zero training classification error is not established by readable values in the supplied text. Figure 6 includes training accuracy, but its extracted axes do not establish the achieved accuracy. Corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, and size-dependent interpolation are not tested.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth-dependent training degradation and matched comparisons of plain and residual networks.
Activation-matched initialization, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, training speed, and trainable depth.

Recovery from learning rates above the initial linearized-model stability limit, the larger-rate divergence boundary, and divergence from initially subthreshold runs are not directly tested. The main tracked experiments stop before a second unstable eigenvalue; the theorem provides local coupling rather than global convergence.
Matched batch-normalization comparisons and normalization-free Fixup training.

missing.what: The study's explicit progressive-sharpening example: an MLP trained on CIFAR-10 at η = 0.02 reaches instability after approximately 2200 steps, then sharpness hovers near 100 while training continues.

Additional loss-and-sharpness trajectories across learning rates: MLP and CNN with MSE on CIFAR-10; CNN with logistic loss on cats versus dogs; ResNet18 with MSE on cats versus dogs; Transformer with MSE and logistic loss on SST2. These are omitted empirical conditions, even though their results are mainly graphical.

The observed transition from subquadratic to superquadratic behavior and the generalized prediction of limiting sharpness below or above 2/η. Record this threshold-offset evidence separately from whether the prediction method succeeds.

The multiple-unstable-eigenvalue experiment: successive eigenvalues become unstable and dynamics become more chaotic. This bears on behavior beyond the main experiments' stopping condition; increased chaos alone does not establish failure of V5.

record.verdict_notes: Failure of the cubic prediction in some architectures or losses limits that explanatory approximation, not V5 itself. Likewise, the single-eigenvalue analysis and stopping rule leave broader behavior untested rather than demonstrating a claim failure. No numerical curve endpoints are inferred from extracted axis labels.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, and model width comparisons are not tested.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student local-minimum or width comparison.
No plain-versus-residual shortcut comparison or depth sweep testing training error.

The study tests full-batch gradient descent at the edge of stability and larger learning rates on selected architectures and datasets. It does not test the full set of wide-network squared-loss settings, initial linearized-model stability limits, or divergence cases described in V5.
No batch-normalization comparison or normalization-free Fixup test.

rows.subject: 3-layer MLP

rows.measure: Training loss and sharpness over training steps
rows.note: Text says Figure 4 confirms that the predicted dynamics accurately predict loss and sharpness, and that gradient descent and constrained trajectories remain close throughout training.
rows.check: The relevant result is decreasing loss over longer times while sharpness fluctuates near 2/η = 1000, rather than prediction accuracy itself. Figure 4 reports two-step-averaged sharpness. Appendix D specifies swish activation and stopping when the constrained trajectory's second eigenvalue reaches 1.9/η.
